metadata.file_name: 140. Herborn et al. (2020). The Assessment of Collaborative Problem Solving in PISA 2015: Can Computer Agents Replace Humans?.pdf
metadata.title: The Assessment of Collaborative Problem Solving in PISA 2015: Can Computer Agents Replace Humans?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a classroom-based validation design with a convenience sample of German secondary grammar school students (Grades 9–10) who completed four PISA 2015 CPS tasks in constrained human-to-agent (H-A) and/or constrained human-to-human (H-H) formats. The manuscript reports exclusions for missing values and pilot-study participants, but it does not describe the use of PISA-style complex survey weights or any sampling-weight variables in the analyses. Because the analyses are based on confirmatory factor modeling and MANOVA comparisons rather than population-representative estimation, the paper does not provide a weight variable to apply; therefore, results should be interpreted as validity evidence for the task interface rather than nationally representative CPS estimates. Missingness was handled via multiple imputation (50 imputations) due to the planned missing-by-design structure from the group-based task-order design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables are CPS correctness scores and behavioral action counts derived from the study’s constrained administration of PISA 2015 CPS tasks, rather than PV-based achievement scales produced by the PISA scoring model. The paper instead uses multiple imputation to address missing-by-design data from the group-based task completion structure, and it reports validity via factor-structure models and interface comparisons rather than PV-based achievement estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were recruited in Germany from eight secondary grammar schools; students were in Grades 9 and 10 (PISA population). A total of N=748 students in 35 classes participated initially; the final analytic sample included 386 students after exclusions for missing informed-consent forms, exclusion of N=71 students from pilot studies, exclusion of data missing by design due to the group-based task-order plan, and exclusion of two students due to missing values. Students were also restricted to main test takers only for the analyses addressing RQ1 and RQ2; students in the role of collaboration partners were excluded. Each student completed four of the seven available PISA 2015 CPS tasks due to time constraints, and each student’s H-A/H-H format exposure followed the group-specific sequence (Groups 1–4), creating planned missingness across tasks.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict problem solving, finding that The study validates the PISA 2015 collaborative problem solving (CPS) human-to-agent (H-A) interface by comparing it to a constrained human-to-human (H-H) format where one computer agent is replaced by a real classmate while keeping the predefined chat structure. Using a German classroom sample (final N=386; Grades 9–10), the authors tested factorial validity with consecutive confirmatory factor models in Mplus and found support for a general CPS factor across H-A and H-H items, with no evidence that interface-specific method factors were needed. For performance accuracy, multivariate tests (MANOVA; Pillai’s trace) showed no significant interface effect on CPS correctness across four tasks (V=0.02, F(4,186)=0.77, p=.548). For behavioral actions, interface significantly affected the number of actions (V=0.11, F(4,186)=5.55, p<.001), with classmates producing slightly more actions on Tasks 1 and 2 but not on Tasks 3–4. Limitations include the constrained nature of the H-H condition (predefined chat options; no free chat) and the fact that the sample is not population-representative for Germany. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an ML prediction/classification paper: the study uses confirmatory factor modeling (SEM/measurement validity) and MANOVA to compare interface effects on CPS correctness and behavioral action counts. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms, no ML target variable, and no predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) to extract; the main empirical contribution is construct validity and interface comparability rather than supervised learning.
